strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP safety problem through substantial empirical coverage: 17 attacks, nine LLMs, 16 violation categories, and eight defenses. Comparing attack performance before and after external filtering provides useful evidence beyond standalone attack demonstrations.

The automatic evaluator receives meaningful human validation: three annotators assess 640 responses, with Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87 and reported evaluator agreement of 94.84%. Explicitly checking for question restatements addresses a concrete weakness of simpler success criteria.

Transfer experiments, token and runtime measurements, and seven months of longitudinal evaluation broaden the contribution beyond an ASR leaderboard. Detailed results expose considerable variation across models and violation categories.

Explicit category definitions, provider-policy mappings, and manual screening make the dataset construction understandable. The paper also acknowledges limitations concerning changing policies, model coverage, and harmful-response quality.
weaknesses: The central explanation that seed dependence causes poor robustness is insufficiently established. Sections 6–8 infer this mechanism from comparisons between different algorithms, without controlling seed diversity, prompt length, or optimizer choice. The taxonomy also has overlapping criteria: heuristic optimization can use feedback. These observations support hypotheses about the tested implementations, but not the broad recommendation to deprioritize heuristic attacks.

The defense evaluation lacks benign-query false-positive rates and utility measurements, and does not clearly specify whether attacks are reoptimized against the complete defended pipeline. Consequently, near-zero ASR under Prompt-Guard or combined defenses establishes limited detectability results without adequately supporting the claimed practical ineffectiveness of entire attack families.

The claimed unified comparison has important limitations. Fifty prompt modifications and 500 gradient steps do not establish comparable query or compute budgets; GE’s success over 50 generation settings further requires an explicit accounting of selection and evaluation budgets. More concretely, Table 13 and Appendix G.7 replace MasterKey’s defining fine-tuning procedure with GPT-4 rewriting AIM. This surrogate should not support conclusions about the original method or fine-tuning-based attacks generally.

The interpretation of ASR overstates what the benchmark measures. The union of provider usage policies includes deployment obligations, such as disclosure and professional review, whose violation cannot always be inferred from an isolated response. Although policy differences are acknowledged, aggregate results are used to characterize individual models’ alignment failures. Table 3 reports baseline success of 78–94% in six categories; provider-specific analyses and success conditional on initial refusal would better distinguish existing compliance from successful safeguard bypass.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for the proposed benchmark. The supplied manuscript provides neither the complete 160-question dataset nor an identifiable evaluation artifact, and Figure 9 explicitly omits the judge’s actual few-shot demonstrations. The 50 GE configurations are not enumerated. Repetition counts and uncertainty estimates are also missing despite stochastic attacks and only ten questions per category. Together with the comparison and interpretation issues above, these are important, repairable gaps that motivate resubmission next cycle.
